claims.text: The starting material is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a solution-treated simple solid-solution state.
Cooling rate after solution treatment modulates the degree of short-range atomic order in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Slow cooling promotes more short-range atomic order than rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching produces a baseline state with minimal short-range atomic order.
Greater short-range atomic order increases lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion impedes dislocation migration and creates barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy strength and hardness.
Short-range atomic ordering governs the balance among deformation behavior, hardness, and compressive strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Slow-cooled specimens will have higher Vickers hardness than fast-quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled specimens will have higher compressive strength than fast-quenched specimens at room temperature.
Slow-cooled specimens will have higher compressive strength than fast-quenched specimens at 600 °C.
The increased ordering and strength of slow-cooled specimens may be accompanied by a modest decrease in ductility.
Rapidly quenched specimens will have lower strength but greater plasticity than slow-cooled specimens.
Mechanical-property differences will correlate directly with the measured degree of short-range order.
TEM and diffraction measurements can detect and quantify the proposed short-range-order differences.
The comparison is intended to hold chemistry and microstructure other than ordering constant while changing cooling rate.
The proposed scope is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested in compression from room temperature through 600 °C.
